# telly

> Five television channels built from one person's YouTube subscriptions. Each
> has its own schedule, its own hours and its own taste. They join programmes
> already in progress and show a test card when nothing is on. You do not pick
> what to watch; you switch the set on, press a preset, and see what is on.

telly is a browser-only single-page app, served as static files from GitHub
Pages, with no backend, no server and no server-side database of its own. It
signs in with Google Identity Services, reads the visitor's own subscriptions
with the `youtube.readonly` scope, and plays them in YouTube's own embedded
player. The access token is kept in the tab's own session storage, so that
reloading the page does not sign the visitor out, until the lifetime Google
gives it runs out; the app never logs it and never puts it in a URL. What telly
reads from YouTube is saved in the visitor's own browser, in IndexedDB, under a
key carrying their account's channel id. Signing out revokes the grant at
Google and removes that account's saved copy.

## The one idea

Wall-clock time is the only input. The app never asks *what shall we play
next?* It asks **what should be on air at 14:32:07, and how far into it are
we?** That question gives join-in-progress, closedown, overruns and the test
card for nothing, and collapses the whole thing into two pure functions:

    plan(pool, options) -> Schedule   // deterministic, once per broadcast day
    tune(schedule, now) -> OnAir      // pure, called every tick

The broadcast day runs 06:00 to 06:00. News junctions start on time; everything
else may overrun and push the day along. Gaps become the test card.

## Five stations

Subscriptions are divided between five broadcasters and belong to one each.
Which station a channel goes to comes from what YouTube says it is about;
when it goes out comes from how long its videos run, how often it posts and how
well watched it is. Nothing age-rated goes out before nine and nothing made for
children goes out after six. One station opens at eleven, another at three in
the afternoon, and a fifth never closes down at all.

## The set

The television itself is drawn, not photographed: the teak cabinet, the
bakelite keys and the aluminium fascia are SVG filters, so there are no image
assets. The controls work: volume, six channel presets, and five trimmers
behind the flap. V and H are the frame and line oscillators, and turning either
off its lock rolls or tears the picture. B is black level, C is saturation, and
T is the tuner, which loses the colour before it loses the picture. Two presets
were set carelessly and have to be found with the tuner; the sixth has no
station on it at all.
